description: Solo participant building a public facing web tool for NASA’s SPHEREx competition
summary: SkyDrift turns SPHEREx's all-sky images into a blink comparator anyone can use. Enter a sky position (or tap a preset) and watch that patch of sky across visits months apart, so stars that move or change stand out. Because SPHEREx sees every spot at a different wavelength in each exposure, a naive blink flickers for no real reason. SkyDrift stacks each detector per visit, so only real changes remain. It then flags movers and variables automatically and checks its own measurements against known nearby stars.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SkyDrift shows SPHEREx images of any sky position as a blink: per-visit stacks for each of the six detectors (0.75-5 microns), single exposures labeled with their wavelength, an all-epoch stack, and a difference image. Every frame is labeled with date, days since the first frame, wavelength, observation IDs, release and flagged-pixel statistics. Settings live in the URL, and an "Embed this view" button gives an iframe snippet. A static version of five presets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855-0714, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) runs with no server; arbitrary positions need the local server.

HOW IT WORKS

Exposures covering a position are found and cutouts fetched from IRSA. Zodiacal light is subtracted and pixels are masked with the SPHEREx team's documented photometry flag list. Everything is reprojected to a common north-up 3.1"/pixel grid, then stacked per visit and detector with inverse-variance weights, using one shared stretch per sequence. Because SPHEREx sees each spot at a different wavelength in every exposure, a naive blink flickers for no real reason; stacking per visit and detector keeps the comparison wavelength-fair, so only real changes remain.

AUTOMATIC CANDIDATES

Sources are detected in each visit stack and matched between the first and last visits, and the field's median offset is removed. Movers are shifts above 5 sigma, confirmed by a +/- pair in the difference image. Variables are flux changes above 5 sigma, claimed only where the two visits cover overlapping wavelengths.

RESULTS SO FAR (REAL SPHEREx DATA)

- WISE 0855-0714 (the coldest known brown dwarf) is detected near 4.6 microns and invisible near 1 micron. Its motion is recovered in detector D6: about 4 arcseconds in 5.5 months, matching the predicted direction (measured 4.07" vs predicted 4.61", position angle 281 vs 277 degrees).

- RW Aurigae is flagged as variable: flux x1.7 relative to the field, at overlapping wavelengths.

- Truth check: 48 measurements of 29 known high-proper-motion stars, 35 consistent with the prediction. Vector RMS 0.85" for the consistent measurements and 1.86" over all, outliers kept (one SPHEREx pixel is 6.2").

WHY IT IS DIFFERENT

Most blinkers just flip between images. SkyDrift is built so the blink is fair across wavelengths, finds movers and variables automatically, and tests its own measurements against known stars, so users can see how far to trust it.

HONEST LIMITS

IRSA's query services (TAP/SIA/cone search) were down during the whole build, so SkyDrift finds data by reading file headers from IRSA's public S3 bucket, a sampled search that can miss some exposures. Comparison proper motions are literature values, not live Gaia queries. Bright stars such as Barnard's Star saturate. Candidates are candidates, not discoveries.

TOOLS

Python (astropy, astroquery, numpy, scipy, reproject, sep, pillow, imageio, matplotlib, requests, FastAPI, uvicorn, pytest) and a plain HTML/JavaScript front end. Data: SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images (DR1 and QR3) from NASA/IPAC IRSA.

USE OF AI

AI-assisted, human-led. I led this project from idea to release I set the goals, made the engineering decisions, tested the results, and shipped it. The code was written with AI assistance (Claude Code, Anthropic), working from specifications and prompts I directed. No AI-generated images or video, and no NASA branding. The specification and selected prompts are in docs/prompts/.
dataRefs: SPHEREx spectral images, NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (DR1 and QR3)
projectRefs: Gaia DR3, ESA (literature proper motions and parallaxes)
